39 pages. v2: substantially revised and retitled (v1 title: "LLMEval-Logic: A Solver-Verified Chinese Benchmark for Logical Reasoning of LLMs with Adversarial Hardening"); new construction pipeline, data tiers, and experiments

This repository and the [Hugging Face dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/tencent/HyperLogic) go public with about 30% of the items of every tier, their gold answers, the direct-answer prompt and scorer, and the complete Hard agent evaluation
The paper is released on arXiv as HyperLogic (v2 of arXiv:2605.19597) — HyperLogic-Base with 195 items and 922 sub-questions, HyperLogic-Hard with 100 items, and results for 7 frontier models.
The construction pipeline separates problem authoring from answer generation. A multi-agent workflow hardens Chinese seeds written by logic-trained undergraduates, **without solving them**.
an item is released only when its two corrected encodings agree
Because the solvers do the search, items can be harder than the models that built them, while every answer stays executable and auditable.

**HyperLogic-Seed** — 228 single-question seeds written by undergraduates with coursework in logic. Like existing benchmarks, Seed barely separates frontier models: all seven are within 5.9 points of each other.
**HyperLogic-Base** — 195 items, each a shared background (about 3,300 Chinese characters) with 4.7 sub-questions on average. An item counts as correct only if every sub-question is.

**HyperLogic-Hard** — 100 single-question items with larger, coupled search spaces (backgrounds of about 8,700 characters). Direct solving is no longer practical; Hard also evaluates agents that write code in a sandbox, with or without our logic modeling library.

Excludes items refused by the model's API service. Grok 4.6 runs at `xhigh`, every other model at `max`. Models are ranked by Base item accuracy.

On five of seven existing logic benchmarks, three frontier models differ by at most three points, and Seed behaves the same way (83.9–89.8%). On Base every model loses at least 12 points from Seed and the seven models spread over 33.0 points (44.6–77.6%).
Median reasoning length on Base ranges from 15.2k to 52.7k tokens per item and does not track accuracy
No model exceeds 16% directly. A code sandbox lifts every model by 16.7–40.1 points, yet the best reaches only 55.7% (57.0% with the library).
With a sandbox alone, six of seven models mostly write plain Python that enumerates candidate assignments and filters them with handwritten rules.

A benchmark whose every item is public stops measuring reasoning once its items enter training data. So we release a fixed, uniformly sampled **30% of the items of each tier**, together with everything needed to run the evaluation, and keep the rest private:
**Public items with gold answers**: `data/seed.json`, `data/base.json`, and `data/hard.json`. Samples are item-level: all sub-questions of a selected Base item are kept together.
the full 11-module `translation` library and `MANUAL.md` given to the library condition.
**The selection procedure** in `build_public_subset.py` and `selection_manifest.json`, with SHA-256 commitments to the full corpus, so the split can be audited.

The remaining 70% of the items and the expert-validated formal translations of **all** items, public ones included, are held out. Scores on the public subset cannot reproduce the full-benchmark numbers above
Missing and invalid predictions count as wrong; refusals are reported separately and excluded from the denominator, as in the paper.
The paper uses a semantic-equivalence LLM judge, not literal string matching; `evaluate.py` judges all sub-questions of an item together.
Every item has `id`, `background`, aligned `question[]` and `answer[]` arrays, and optionally `title`.
No formal translations, author information, or private items are included.

The held-out 70% of HyperLogic is not public, so that results on it stay free of contamination. To have a model evaluated on the full benchmark, [contact us](#-contact), and we will run it under the same protocol as the leaderboard.

Huang, Xuanjing and Chen, Alex and Pan, Maxm},
Forward construction preserves the challenge of finding a faithful formalization, yet makes difficulty and answer reliability harder to control.
We introduce HyperLogic, a forward-construction pipeline that separates problem authoring from answer generation.

A multi-agent workflow hardens undergraduate-authored Chinese seeds without solving them; two agents from different model families independently translate each finished item into executable finite-domain models; their encodings and solver-derived answers undergo layered, agent-assisted adjudication under human-expert oversight.
HyperLogic-Base contains 195 items and 922 sub-questions and separates seven frontier models by 33.0 percentage points in strict item accuracy (44.6-77.6%).
HyperLogic-Hard contains 100 items with larger, coupled search spaces, on which no model exceeds 16% accuracy in direct answering.
The sandbox improves every model by 16.7-40.1 points; adding the library helps five models and hurts two.
Most scalable logic benchmarks use reverse construction: they begin with a formal structure and render it into natural language,
Choosing a faithful model is itself part of the reasoning task, and reverse construction largely removes this step.

Table 2 makes the saturation concrete: five of seven benchmarks separate three frontier models by at most three points, and three are already at 97–100%; HyperLogic-Base opens that spread to 32.0 points.
More broadly, existing logical-reasoning benchmarks primarily measure direct-answer performance, with relatively little attention to agents' ability to solve logical problems using tools.
In direct answering no model exceeds 16%; a code sandbox lifts every model by 17 to 40 points, while adding the logic modeling library raises five models and lowers two.
We therefore choose forward construction.
A hardening agent workflow rewrites an input item under a selected strategy library.
The library specifies the reasoning mechanisms to introduce and the intended difficulty tier; the four agent roles plan, implement, and review those mechanisms.
The workflow consists of four nodes (Appendix A.2):
Library-Base produces items within the models' ceiling.
Its six operators make the reasoning longer: more branches to follow, more distractor premises to rule out, more sub-questions to answer, more aliases to keep track of.
Library-Hard produces items past the point of direct solving.

It retains four Library-Base operators as carriers and adds four hardening axes—minimality cores, global coupling constraints, cyclic truth reference, and coupled state dimensions—each with four implementations; Appendices A.3 and A.4 list both libraries in full.
To obtain auditable gold answers without requiring the authoring agents to solve the items, we translate each item into a finite-domain theory and evaluate its queries with logic solvers.
To make these translations uniform and auditable, we give every formalization agent the same logic modeling library.
The library supports six query modalities
uniqueness, enumeration, exact counting, and incompatibility.
Answers are computed under the scopes specified by the question.
The encodings, the answers, and the agents' authoring traces are the inputs to expert audit (Section 2.4).
Before accepting solver-derived answers as gold, we audit the encodings against the original background and questions.
Two independently produced encodings can share a misreading even when their answers agree.
Faulty encodings are corrected and rerun; ambiguous items are clarified or excluded.
Release requires matching substantive answers from the two reviewed encodings.
Automated checks identify potential defects, and a human logic expert reviews the evidence and resolves discrepancies with agent assistance.
The review also examines agreeing answers for shared misinterpretations.

Figure 5 groups attempts with saved code into three routes: code referencing the logic modeling library, code importing an independent symbolic solver, and plain Python code with neither detected.
In the sandbox-only condition, six of seven models predominantly write plain Python.
For five models, it accounts for 78%–89% of coded attempts; DeepSeek V4 Pro uses it in 67%, while GPT-5.6 Sol splits almost evenly between plain Python and an imported solver.
These Python programs commonly enumerate candidate assignments and filter them with handwritten rules.
Access to a sandbox alone therefore seldom leads models to choose a symbolic solver.

When the logic modeling library and its manual are available, the share of coded attempts containing either library code or an independently imported solver rises by 19–45 percentage points for every model.

We used generative AI tools for benchmark construction and evaluation, including hardening human … authored seeds, translating items into formal models, assisting with auditing and repairs, judging model responses, and categorizing errors.

AI tools also assisted with methodological feedback, checking formal definitions, implementing and debugging code, analyzing and interpreting results, preparing figures, and drafting and revising the manuscript.
Reference answers are computed by logic solvers and checked through the audit procedure under human-expert oversight described in Section 2.4.
The authors retain responsibility for the benchmark, the reported results and claims, and the final manuscript.
A human logic expert reviews the original item, both encodings, their solver-derived answers, the translation traces, and available check reports.
Among questions with initially agreeing answers, 27.0% required corrections to both encodings, showing that answer agreement can conceal shared misinterpretations.
Among questions with initially disagreeing answers, 81.1% required correction to one encoding, and 95.8% reached matching substantive answers after repair or confirmation of equivalent notation.
Only items that pass expert review are included in the dataset.
We combine independent translations by two models, multiple layers of auditing, and human-expert review to check semantic fidelity and answer consistency as thoroughly as possible.

Translating natural-language problems into formal representations remains vulnerable to misinterpretation, and correct solver execution does not guarantee that the resulting answers faithfully reflect the original text.

Nevertheless, these checks cannot provide an absolute guarantee of correctness: shared misinterpretations, overlooked ambiguities, or annotation errors may remain in the released items and reference answers.
